questions.question: For a work-conserving single-server queue, which time interval is a busy period $U$?
options: From the arrival of a job until that same job departs.
From the start of a job's service until that service ends.
From an arrival that finds the system empty until the server next becomes idle.
From an arrival that finds the system empty until the waiting line first empties.

questions.question: In a work-conserving single-server queue the server alternates between busy periods $U$ and idle periods $I$. Which time interval is one idle period $I$?
options: The time from the end of a busy period until the next arrival.
The time between two consecutive arrivals at the queue.
The time a job spends waiting in line before its service starts.
The total time in $[0,t]$ during which the system is empty.

questions.question: A busy period of a work-conserving single server starts at the arrival time $A_1$ of job $1$ and serves jobs $1,\dots,n$ with $n\geq2$, with arrival times $A_k$, service times $S_k$ and departure times $D_k$. Which expression equals its length $U$?
options: $D_n-A_n$
$S_1+S_2+\dots+S_n$

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda$, the mean idle period is $\mathbb{E}[I]=1/\lambda$, even though an idle period starts some time after the last arrival. Which argument justifies this?
options: The idle period is a whole inter-arrival time, as the last job of the busy period arrives just when the busy period ends.
The idle period mirrors the first service of the busy period, and that service has mean $1/\lambda$ when $\rho<1$.
For any arrival process with rate $\lambda$, the time from any fixed instant to the next arrival has mean $1/\lambda$.
Exponential inter-arrival times are memoryless, so the time from the end of a busy period to the next arrival has mean $1/\lambda$.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue the mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ is kept fixed and the arrival rate $\lambda$ is lowered so that the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ tends to $0$. What happens to the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$?
options: $\mathbb{E}[U]$ tends to $0$, because the server is hardly ever busy.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ tends to $1/\lambda$, the typical gap between arrivals.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ tends to $\mathbb{E}[S]$, since most busy periods serve a single job.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ is close to $\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, the busy fraction times $\mathbb{E}[S]$.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at an $M/G/1$ queue at rate $\lambda=4$ per hour, and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=10$ minutes. What is the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$?
options: $30$ minutes
$15$ minutes
$20$ minutes
$10/3\approx3.3$ minutes

questions.question: A single server with general service times, mean $\mathbb{E}[S]=12$ minutes, receives a Poisson stream of $4$ jobs per hour ($M/G/1$). On average, how long does each idle period $I$ between two busy periods last?
options: $60$ minutes
$12$ minutes
$3$ minutes
$15$ minutes

questions.question: A work-conserving FIFO single server receives jobs at times $0,1,3,7,7.5$ with service times $2,1.5,1,1,2$ (departures at $2,3.5,4.5,8,10$). What are the lengths of the busy periods on $[0,10]$?
options: $10$ (one busy period)

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue with load $\rho=0.8$, let $N$ be the number of jobs served in one busy period. What is $\mathbb{E}[N]$?
For which of these single-station queues, written in Kendall's notation with load $\rho$, may the busy-period formula $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ be used?
options: $D/M/1$ with $\rho=0.6$
$M/G/2$ with $\rho=0.6$
$M/M/1$ with $\rho=1.2$
$M/D/1$ with $\rho=0.6$

questions.question: For the $M/G/1$ queue with $\rho<1$, the mean busy period satisfies $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]+\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[U]$. What does the term $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[U]$ account for?
options: With probability $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ one job arrives during the first service and starts a busy period of mean $\mathbb{E}[U]$.
On average $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ jobs arrive during the first service, and each starts its own busy period of mean $\mathbb{E}[U]$.
On average $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ jobs arrive during the first service, and each adds only its own service time to $U$.
The first job of the busy period waits on average $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[U]$ before its service starts.

questions.question: The $M/G/1$ derivation of $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]+\rho\,\mathbb{E}[U]$ treats each job arriving during the first service as starting its own busy period, cleared one after another. A FIFO server does not serve the jobs in such blocks. Why does the equation still hold under FIFO?
options: The busy-period length is the total service time of its jobs, which does not depend on the order of service.
Under FIFO the sojourn time of each job equals the busy period that it starts, so the blocks coincide.
With $\rho<1$ at most one job arrives during the first service, so the order of service never matters.
Exponential service times are memoryless, so the order in which jobs are served is irrelevant.

questions.question: A job is served in a busy period of length $U$ of a work-conserving FIFO single server. Which relation between the job's sojourn time $J$ and $U$ always holds?
options: $J=U$ whenever the job is the one that starts the busy period.
$J\geq U$ when the job is the last one served, as it waits for all others.
$J$ equals the total service time of the job itself and all jobs served before it in that busy period.
$J\leq U$, because the job's whole stay lies inside the busy period.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue the mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ is fixed, and the arrival rate increases so that the load rises from $\rho=0.8$ to $\rho=0.9$. By what factor does the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$ change?
An $M/G/1$ queue is observed to have mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]=40$ minutes and mean idle period $\mathbb{E}[I]=10$ minutes. What is the mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: $8$ minutes
$36$ minutes
$10$ minutes
$32$ minutes

questions.question: An $M/G/1$ queue has load $\rho=1.25$. Substituting into $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ gives $-4\,\mathbb{E}[S]$. Which statement about the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$ is correct?
options: $\mathbb{E}[U]=4\,\mathbb{E}[S]$; the minus sign only signals that $\rho$ exceeds one.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ is finite, but the mean idle period $\mathbb{E}[I]$ becomes infinite.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ is finite if the service times are exponential, and infinite otherwise.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ is not finite: $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]+\rho\,\mathbb{E}[U]$ has no finite positive solution.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue the arrival rate $\lambda$ is fixed while the mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ increases so that $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ approaches $1$ from below. What happens to the mean idle period $\mathbb{E}[I]$ and the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$?
options: $\mathbb{E}[I]$ shrinks towards $0$ as the server is rarely idle, while $\mathbb{E}[U]$ grows.
$\mathbb{E}[U]$ grows only in proportion to $\mathbb{E}[S]$, and $\mathbb{E}[I]$ stays at $1/\lambda$.
$\mathbb{E}[I]$ stays at $1/\lambda$, while $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ grows without bound.
Both grow like $1/(1-\rho)$, so their ratio $\mathbb{E}[U]/\mathbb{E}[I]$ stays constant.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single server exactly every $2$ minutes, from time $0$ on, and each needs exactly $1.5$ minutes of service, so $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ per minute and $\rho=0.75$. Which statement about the actual busy period $U$, the actual idle period $I$ and the $M/G/1$ values $\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ and $1/\lambda$ is correct?
options: Actual $U=6$ and $I=2$, matching the formulas since $\rho<1$.
Actual $U=1.5$ and $I=0.5$; the formulas would give $6$ and $2$.
Actual $U=1.5$ and $I=2$; only the busy-period formula fails.
Actual $U=2$ and $I=0$, as each job arrives when the previous one leaves.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at an $M/G/1$ queue at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute. Each service time is $0.5$ or $2.5$ minutes, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. What is the mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[U]$?
options: $6$ minutes, from $\mathbb{E}[S]=1.5$ and $\rho=0.75$
Not finite, as the $2.5$-minute jobs give load $1.25$
$3$ minutes, from $\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\lambda)$ with $\lambda=0.5$
$1.5$ minutes, the mean service time of one job
